heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Literature Review, 1.2 Restatement of the Tasks)
note: One 308-word literature block, then the five ICM tasks. Block 23 both defines EDP (people whose homeland becomes uninhabitable because of environmental stressors such as climate change) and lists the work it draws on, and it runs straight into the '1.2 Restatement of the Tasks' heading without a break, so the chapter has no separate definition paragraph and no gap between literature and task statement. The tasks are simplified rather than restated: each is given as a headline sentence and every task is split over two measured blocks because its wrapped line is its own block (25/26, 27/28, 31/32). Task 2 is reworded to 'human rights and cultural preservation', Task 3 to 'models to measure the potential impact of our proposed policies', and the five-task list ends inside block 32, which also carries the '2 Analysis of the Issue Paper' heading. No task is quoted from the problem sheet, and no scope number (how many people, which countries) appears in the chapter at all - the only figures the paper will use arrive in the model chapters.

heading: 2 Analysis of the Issue Paper (2.1 survival at risk, 2.2 loss of cultural heritage)
note: The scope answer to Task 1 is two lists of bullets hung on one mindmap. Block 33 announces the 'prospectives', block 34 is the Figure 1 caption (the mindmap itself is never read), and the two subsections then state, without measurement, what the paper will later model. 2.1: climate change -> CO2 -> greenhouse effect -> sea-level rise -> salinisation and flooding -> no food -> no country (block 36, a causal chain with no number); the receiving country's carrying capacity may not meet EDP needs, and block 38 is the only definition in the chapter, 'the maximum population size that the environment can sustain indefinitely'; block 39 argues that the migration must be planned on a time scale because the loss accumulates slowly - a planning argument, not a quantity, hence ext:context. 2.2: block 41 defines the three heritage types (tangible movable/immovable, intangible, natural); block 42 argues protection is obligatory even under the housing-first premise through a menu-cost analogy ('if a manufacturer changes the price ... All this incurs a new cost') which is asserted, not applied - no cost is computed; block 43 selects the three receiving-country attributes the policy must weigh (social stability, cultural diversity, nationalist orientation). Block 43 also carries the '3 The Wandering Homeland Policy' heading in its tail. The chapter's only support is the Figure 2 caption (heights above sea level by city), whose data is cited to five web sources and never used numerically.

heading: 3 The 'Wandering Homeland Policy' (motivation, 3.1 assumptions, 3.2 the statement of the policy)
note: One transition block, three assumptions, eight policy clauses. The assumptions are all scope restrictions and all one sentence: the policy covers only sea-level EDPs and not hurricane/flood/earthquake refugees; every EDP consents to move; the world stays politically stable. None is justified and the third is the one the whole receiving-country allocation rests on. The clauses: (i) every country has an obligation to assist, grounded in 'community of shared future for mankind' rather than in a duty rule; (ii) the assistance instrument is Direct assistance, with the receiving country paying; (iii) responsibility is allocated by four indicators - greenhouse gas emission, GDP per capita, arable land per capita, renewable freshwater per capita - which is the input list Model 2 will use, so this clause is the actual design decision of the paper; (iv) non-refoulement under international human rights law is cited as the legal basis for resettlement or citizenship, and this is the only clause with a legal source; (v) classifies culture into movable and immovable material plus intangible; (vi)-(viii) hand the work to named actors - UNESCO and local governments for relocatable material culture via consultation, donation, museum collection and auction; UNESCO and local governments again for non-removable heritage via data collection, technical protection and remote reproduction; receiving countries for an open protective policy. Clauses i-viii are numbered in the text but the measurement breaks the numbering across blocks only at (viii), whose block also carries the '4 Notations' heading.

heading: 4 Notations (Table 1)
note: Table 1 is thirteen measured blocks because every row is its own block: EDP, UNHCR, h0, R0, h, r, delta-h, rho0, gamma, t, v, N_EDP(t), GG, AL, RFR. The table caption and the lead sentence 'The primary notations used in this paper are listed in Table 1' sit in block 58 and the table body runs to block 70, whose tail carries the '5 The Models' heading. Coded as one group because the measurement split one table row by row. Note the table is the only place where the cone geometry symbols are declared, and it declares h (altitude of a point on the cone) and r (latest base radius) without saying whether they are the flooded or the unflooded part - the model chapter has to be read to recover that.

heading: 5.1 Model 1: The number of EDPs by geometry
note: The one model in the paper that can be checked end to end. Inputs: sea level rises linearly at 3.44 mm/year (block 72, cited), and 65 million people will live in developing island nations by 2070 at density 444/km2 and growth 2.3% (block 77, cited); the four problem countries (Maldives, Tuvalu, Kiribati, ...) are taken as representatives. Geometry: the island is a cone of original height h0 and base radius R0 whose base area equals the four nations' total area; k1 = h0/R0, and since delta-h = vt, eq (5) gives r(t) = R0 - vt/k1. Then S(t) = pi[R0^2 - r^2(t)], dS(t) = pi[r^2(t-1) - r^2(t)], and eq (8) N_EDP(t) = rho(t) dS(t) = (1+gamma)^(t-1) rho0 pi[r^2(t-1) - r^2(t)]. Two steps are worth naming. The 65 million figure is a stock for 2070, but the model produces an annual flow and the paper simply sums 50 years of flows to 18,230,968 EDPs (block 91); nothing reconciles the flow sum with the stock that the density and growth rate were calibrated to, and the 18.2M is roughly a quarter of the 65M it started from. And the cone substitution sets rho0 to the density of all island nations while the cone's base is only the four problem countries, so density and area are drawn from different populations. Blocks 74-90 are split one line at a time by the inline equations (74/75/76 are eq (1) and its two symbol bullets; 85/86 and 87/88 are single equations cut mid-symbol), which is why four derivation groups cover twelve blocks.

heading: 5.2 Model 2: Distribution of EDPs among responsible countries by the Entropy Weight Method (5.2.1 indicators, 5.2.2 weights)
note: Selection is a cut, not a model: the top 50 greenhouse-gas emitters for 1970-2018 are declared responsible because they account for 89.7% of world emissions (block 95), under two assumptions - the 50 countries' land is unaffected by sea-level rise, and free trade equalises purchasing power (block 96). The EWM is textbook: normalise v_ij by the column sum (eq 9), E_j = -k sum p_ij ln p_ij with k = ln n (eq 10), q_j = (1-E_j)/sum(1-E_j) (eq 11), n = 50, m = 4. The computed weights are GG 0.259, AL 0.239, GDP 0.139, RFR 0.363 (Table 2, caption block 106, values block 107). Block 108 reads the table as good news ('GG, AL and RFR are highly weighted, which is very close to what we have expected ... the result of the weights is reliable') - but agreement with expectation is not a validity check, and the paper never reports the entropy values or the normalised matrix, only the four final weights. The same block continues into the 50-country score and rank list (block 108 is 216 words and carries the score column vertically), which is the only output of the chapter; the 20 selected receivers appear only as a list, with no stated cut-off rule and no reason given for 20. The score list is not reproducible from the paper: neither the raw indicator matrix nor the normalisation direction (benefit vs cost indicator) is given, and GG enters as a benefit of receiving although higher emissions are the reason for responsibility, not a capacity.

heading: 5.3 Model 3: Competition between foreign and native culture (Lotka-Volterra)
note: Four assumptions (a person has one cultural background only; culture needs people to carry it; the ratio of a group to total population measures a culture; native culture suits national conditions), then variables that make the model a two-species competition: N1 and N2 are the population shares of native and foreign culture, alpha12 the effect of species 2 on 1, alpha21 the reverse, K1 and K2 the carrying capacities. Block 115 writes the standard Lotka-Volterra pair in ratio form and argues that culture competes for the same resources (population, language, geography); block 116 instantiates it for Canada - population fitted logistically over 2000-2019 to 3.8e7 in 2070, 2.97e6 EDPs arriving from Models 1-2, so N1 = 92.7%, N2 = 7.3% - and concludes alpha21 < alpha12. No coefficient is estimated: the sign of the two interaction terms is assumed from the narrative, and the initial shares are the only numbers. Under a UN protection policy the paper sets alpha12 approximately equal to alpha21 (block 118) and Figure 8 then shows the foreign culture surviving longer; block 120 reads the two figures against each other. The comparison is qualitative - 'the implementation of cultural protection policy makes the existence of EDP culture longer' - with no horizon, no equilibrium share, and no sensitivity to the assumed coefficients, so the policy conclusion is set by the assumption that protection raises competitiveness, not by the model.

heading: 5.4 Model 4: The model of economic impact
note: A parameter list, not a derived model. Cost of living per capita C_i comes from a website (block 123); each EDP's annual social value is set at 0.75 of the receiving country's per capita GDP (block 124) with no argument; the labour share is the world 15-64 share, 65.33% (block 125); all labour-capable EDPs work (block 126); value is created only after one year, justified by the EU's one-year resettlement-cost policy (block 127); and per capita resettlement and living costs are identical within a country regardless of age, sex or ethnicity (block 128). Block 129 then declares A_i (per capita resettlement cost), C_i (living cost), M_i (value created) and p_i(t) (new arrivals per year), and its tail carries Table 4 with A_i, C_i, M_i and a country weight column. Block 130 is a handover sentence: 'We use MATLAB to process these datum, and the result and analysis is given in 5.5.' The 0.75 social-value ratio and the one-year lag are the two parameters that decide every sign in 5.5, and neither is sourced or tested; the paper's own conclusion that about half the countries lose money is therefore a statement about 0.75 minus A_i minus C_i, not about EDP economics.

heading: 5.5 Results of the economic benefit of EDPs in 20 receiving countries
note: Five figures, one per income group, each followed by a sentence of reading. Figure 9 gives the aggregate: in the long run there is a clear split, individual developed countries gain obviously, and 'about 1/2 of the countries' have net value below government expenditure - the paper's central and most honest result, stated in one clause of block 134. Then Canada/Australia/US complete the deficit-to-surplus transition in 'more than 2 years' and gain over 5e9 after 50 years (block 137); Japan, Germany, France, UK, Spain and Italy turn positive in two to three years but gain less because their land and resources limit the EDPs allocated to them (block 139); Russia, Brazil, Poland, Korea and Mexico take 4-8 years and still profit (block 141); China, Myanmar, Ukraine, Congo, Indonesia and India stay in deficit throughout (block 143). The mechanism is not discussed: the ranking follows directly from the allocated EDP count and per capita GDP, since value is 0.75 GDP per EDP and costs are fixed per capita, so 'land area and natural resources' is an interpretation of the allocation, not a finding. No table of the 20 countries' 50-year totals is given, only curves, so no reported number can be checked.

heading: 6 The improvements and weaknesses in our policies
note: Five bullets of admitted weakness, all policy-level rather than model-level: the policy counts only direct migrants from sea-level rise and ignores secondary disasters, economic damage and pollution (block 145, which also re-states the 18M result as evidence that the omission is conservative); it ignores differences in national development and the changing international situation, so developing receivers may turn profitable later (block 146); countries in the middle of industrial construction emit more than either poorer or already-industrialised countries and so become responsible receivers while their economies are least able to absorb EDPs (block 147); receiving countries have very limited heritage-protection capacity and need multilateral cooperation (block 148); and the religious composition of EDPs differs from the receiving populations (the block lists Christianity 54%, Islam 30%, Buddhism 6%, Hinduism 2%, non-belief 8% from Wikipedia), so resettlement must consider religion (block 149). Every bullet is a caveat about coverage, none about the geometry model, the EWM weights, the Lotka-Volterra coefficients or the 0.75 value ratio - the four places where the numbers are actually invented. That gap is the most telling thing about the chapter.

heading: 7 The importance and strengths of implementing our policies
note: Four claims tied to the four weakness bullets, one each: the policy fills the legal gap because existing refugee conventions and climate legislation give climate migrants no route to protection by litigation, so the paper proposes a unified UN definition (block 151); basing assistance on responsibility-for-emissions keeps receiving countries from being forced past their capacity, which would otherwise erode willingness (block 152); culture carries values and identity, and the multilateral cooperation mechanism plus a statistical evaluation of undamaged culture is presented as the long-run foundation (block 153); and religion is named as the reason for a resettlement principle for religious EDPs (block 154). The claims restate the policy, not evidence for it: no country has adopted any part, no legal instrument is drafted, and no cost of the multilateral mechanism is estimated. Block 154 also carries the '8 Sensitivity Analysis' heading in its tail.

heading: 8 Sensitivity analysis (sea-level velocity)
note: The only sensitivity test in the paper and it moves one parameter: the sea-level velocity v is set to 3.04, 3.24, 3.44, 3.64 and 3.84 mm/year (block 155), Figure 14 shows the five annual-EDP curves, and block 157 concludes that the trend does not change, so 'our model is stable'. Since N_EDP(t) is linear in v through r(t) = R0 - vt/k1, a 12% change in v can only scale the curve, so the test cannot fail - it checks the functional form the authors themselves chose. Nothing else is varied: not rho0, not gamma, not the 65M stock, not the EWM weights, not the Lotka-Volterra alphas, not the 0.75 social value, which is where the model's real uncertainty sits. The block's tail carries the '9 Conclusion' heading.

heading: 9 Conclusion
note: Six bullets that replay the paper in order: the Issue Paper is analysed and the Wandering Homeland Policy proposed (158); a cone model predicts 18,230,968 EDPs over 50 years (159); four indicators, EWM weights 0.259/0.239/0.139/0.363, 50 scores, and the 20 receivers named (160, which is the only place the full country list appears in one sentence); the economic-impact model gives 50-year income curves and the verdict that the policy suits developed countries but not several developing ones (161); the results are evaluated to improve the policy and its necessity and strengths explained (162); and a sensitivity analysis proves stability (163, whose tail carries 'References'). The conclusion adds no number that is not already in the body, and it repeats 'our model has a good stability' immediately after the paper's own weakness list says some models lack data to test. The 18M figure is restated without its caveat that the 65M stock was the calibration target, and the deficit countries are described as 'not so good' rather than as the roughly half the results chapter reported.
